What I'm working on

Intelligence stopped being the bottleneck a while ago. The harness is what's missing.

Three theses follow from that, and everything I build sits under one of them — the third is where the first two get tested. All of it under Creative Robots, the company I've been running since 2021.

Thesis I

Agents can reason. They can't act.

Every layer of the world checks for a human — a signup form, a consent screen, a credit card, a dashboard. An agent hits the same wall at every level, so I've been building the levels. They stack, bottom-up, and each one plugs into the ones below.

04 Resources
ExtraOrbital
beta

npx extraorbital provision . reads the project, finds the environment variables the code references, creates the real Mongo cluster, S3 bucket, Redis and model keys, and writes them back to .env.local. Every provision is idempotent and takes a lease before calling upstream, so an agent can run it in a retry loop, in CI, on restart, and never double-spend.

no console · no card · ~400 models behind one key · 14 test suites on a real mongod

03 Knowledge
OpenIntegrations
prototype

A registry of every API action in the world, each with an input and output schema, the TypeScript that runs it, the gotchas, and a run button. Call an action nobody has implemented and an agent writes and tests it mid-request — the first call takes a minute, the rest take milliseconds. Reliability is measured rather than asserted: documented → developed → tested → reliable, earned by real runs.

~7.9k providers · ~18.7k actions · 97% success over 50 runs to earn “reliable”

02 Credentials
Keychains
live

Give the agent the keys, not the kingdom. It sends a {{OAUTH2_TOKEN}} placeholder; the proxy resolves the provider, injects the real token, forwards, and streams the response back. The secret never enters the context window, so a prompt injection has nothing to steal. Scopes are inferred per endpoint, since almost no API documents them.

6,000+ APIs · ~1.88M lines of docs mined for scopes · x402 pay-per-call, no account

01 Identity
Interagentic
beta

A machine signs a token with its own key and exchanges it for a ten-minute one addressed to a single service. That service does one JWKS check and learns four things: which machine is calling, whether a human stands behind it, who that human is — a different pseudonym at every service — and what they allowed. Identity is a keypair, not a name: nothing to register, nothing to sign up for at 3am.

10 min tokens, so no revocation protocol · 1 JWKS check per service · 0 secrets held for you

The first attempt at the knowledge layer was skills.dev — a registry of proven, executable skills instead of an LLM rewriting the same integration on every call. It predated Agent Skills; Anthropic shipping them is the clearest validation the idea has had.

Thesis II

Determinism should come from software, not from more tokens.

A model doing by inference what a compiler could do by construction is slower, costlier and less reliable — and unlike the compiler, it has a temperature. Every capability I've moved out of token space and into software space got better on all three.

Layouts.dev
2021 — 2025

A DSL that compiles one parse tree to Next.js and Expo. Concise enough for a designer to read in place of Figma, constrained enough for a model to get right — the grammar has no way to express a side effect or an infinite loop, so validation is parsing rather than linting. We started it in 2021 because GPT-3 was hopeless at React; it turned out to be better DX for humans too.

up to 10× terser than React · 256 visual-test fixtures, web and native · 2 cross-platform headless registries

Slices
launching

Install features, not components. Every registry hands you a beautiful table and wishes you luck — but a table is a view onto a collection, and a collection means auth, an audit trail, a database and a route that filters what each user may see. One shadcn-compatible command writes all six into your repo, and it stays yours.

27 patterns · 6 families · 8 service contracts, 15 swappable implementations, one conformance suite

open-widgets
live

Describe a component, get a real one — installed, typechecked and bundled in a sandbox, embeddable anywhere behind one tag. The generated code never runs on your page.

Thesis III

So take the human out, and watch what breaks.

The first two theses are only worth anything if agents can actually run unsupervised. These are the experiments that tell me where that fails — and they run on everything above.

BotParty
live

Agents forming teams to build an entire company, with their own computers, Slack, Trello and Notion. The question it answers: what do agents do when nobody is prompting them, and at what point does the output stop being trustworthy?

runs on 01 identity · 02 credentials · 04 resources — the integration test for Thesis I

protean
live

The extreme case. A self-evolving agent whose working directory is its own source: it writes new tools for itself, edits its own code, commits, and restarts into the new version. It migrates across machines over P2P, carrying its state on a CRDT. The only constraint left is budget — which is why it needs a supervisor and a crash ladder that walks back through git history until it boots again, because it can and does brick itself.

Try — create an agent, run the command on your own machine, then ask it to photograph you by building the tool first, to spawn itself a server with the AWS CLI, or to spread to a Raspberry Pi on your network.

ux-morph
live

Give every user of your Next.js app their own editable copy of its frontend. Mark a page use morph and each signed-in user gets their own compiled copy: they describe a change in plain language, it is typechecked, and the site rebuilds around them. An experiment, not a product.

Try — pick any persona, then ask it to “Make this look like Win95”.

How I got here

Creative Robots 2021 — now

I built my first vibe-coding product before ChatGPT, when models didn't reliably know how to emit valid JSON. It churned too much to trust, so I spent the two years after that on rail-coding: making AI generate large production applications deterministically, by composing reusable full-stack capabilities instead of re-deriving them. That's where Thesis II comes from, and Layouts.dev is its main output.

Thesis I followed from the thing rail-coding couldn't fix: agents that could write an entire system still couldn't put it online without me. Everything above is the same company, still going.
